However, MIMOS-Tools also supports Simulink models when the deadlines of tasks are set to zero to emulate the zero-time semantics of synchronous design.The toolchain is available atthis http URL.

authors: Riku Kato,Tatsuya Shirai,Olivier Nourry,Yutaro Kashiwa,Kenji Fujiwara,Yasutaka Kamei,Hajimu Iida
title: Raise or Check? Predicting the Necessity of Additional Fuzzing for Continuous Fuzzing
abstract: Continuous fuzzing is used for vulnerability detection in Open Source Software (OSS). Large-scale services such as Google's OSS-Fuzz fuzz over 1,300 projects and have revealed more than 10,000 vulnerabilities. Despite this, a considerable time lag often exists between when a vulnerability is introduced and when it is detected (i.e., the window of exposure). Given the computational cost of additional fuzzing, we aim to allocate fuzzing resources efficiently using vulnerability-risk estimates. We propose RAISE (Risk-Aware Intensive Supplemental Execution Framework), a Just-In-Time (JIT) framework that prioritizes additional fuzzing for high-risk project-days. RAISE performs binary classification at the project-day granularity to estimate whether a vulnerability is introduced on a given day. We construct a dataset combining vulnerability-introducing commits from the OSV database with daily coverage and change metrics from OSS-Fuzz, covering 15 C/C++ projects and 15,210 project-days, of which 347 (2.28%) are vulnerability-introducing. In a cross-project validation setting, our best model, a Random Forest combining VCCFinder-based static features with dynamic fuzzing features, achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.74, substantially outperforming a random baseline; coverage metrics, led by PatchCoverage, are the most important features. In a simulation over 968 vulnerabilities comparing five allocation strategies, Simple-Regression was significantly more cost-efficient than the prediction-agnostic heuristics, spending 91.60 additional fuzzing sessions per detected vulnerability, roughly half the cost of the Median heuristic (171.89). RAISE shows that JIT vulnerability prediction with coverage-aware fuzzing features can effectively guide risk-aware allocation of continuous fuzzing resources.

authors: Yue Xu,Xiyang Wang,Hui Liu,Bolei He
title: From Tokens to Files: Multi-Granularity Detection and Localization of AI-Involved Code
abstract: The increasing use of large language models for code generation calls for methods that distinguish purely human-written code from AI-involved code: files in which any part, however small, was generated or substantially modified by a model. Beyond flagging such files, we aim to localize the lines or blocks attributable to AI. Existing approaches compress a file into a single score, from surface stylistic features or a global code representation, which averages away the evidence when only a few blocks are AI-involved. We propose a framework that models AI authorship at the token level and predicts at the line, block, and file levels. A frozen code language model is equipped with two low-rank adapters, trained separately on machine-written and human-written files; their per-token log-likelihood ratio provides local evidence of AI authorship. Lightweight heads aggregate this evidence within lines and blocks, using the surrounding code context, and their local predictions are aggregated into a file-level decision. We train on mixed-authorship files built from human originals and their AI-generated or AI-modified counterparts, including continuation and fill-in-the-middle scenarios. On an internal test set of 11,773 AI-involved files across six generation regimes against 2,541 human files, our method reaches 72.4 macro F1 at a 1% FPR operating point. With no adaptation, it reaches 62.5 line-level F1 on HybridCodeAuthorship, an external human-AI co-writing benchmark with no training split, above the 56 its own paper reports as the best line-level result. On 19,445 human-written files from repositories created before 2022, the false-positive rate stays between 0.55% and 0.81% under the transported 1% threshold, so the operating point holds on real human code.

authors: Yali Du,Yunji Zhang,Ming Li
title: Hallucinations of Large Language Models in Cross-Language Code Translation: Phenomena and Mitigation
abstract: Code translation converts source code from one programming language to another while preserving its functionality. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have improved code translation, their outputs still contain hallucinations: generated code that conflicts with the source program, violates target-language facts, or introduces contextually inconsistent dependencies. These failures are especially harmful in translation because small semantic deviations can silently change program behavior. Existing hallucination studies mainly focus on natural-language generation or code generation, leaving the forms, distribution, and mitigation of hallucinations in cross-language code translation insufficiently characterized. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of LLM hallucinations in code translation. Across three benchmark datasets, six language pairs, and seven LLMs, we construct a taxonomy with three major categories: Semantic Consistency Conflicts, Factual Knowledge Conflicts, and Project Context Deviations. We manually annotate 13,919 hallucination cases and analyze how hallucination types vary across models, datasets, and language directions. Guided by the taxonomy, we further propose HaluCodeTran, a mitigation framework that combines BM25-based retrieval of relevant translation examples with taxonomy-aware reflective refinement. The study provides an execution-tested characterization of code-translation hallucinations and a practical baseline for building more reliable LLM-based code migration tools.

authors: Siyuan Li,Jiayi Zhou,Zhiyuan Xia,Weijie Wang,Yaowen Zheng,Weiran Tang,Hong Li,Hongsong Zhu,Shanqing Guo
title: A Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning Engine for Compilation-Free Patch Presence Testing
abstract: Code reuse in modern software ecosystems facilitates the spread of 1-day vulnerabilities, posing significant security risks. Determining if patches are present is crucial, but traditional methods suffer from limited usability and accuracy, often depending on a fragile compilation process. In our prior work, we introduced Lares, the first compilation-free framework for patch presence testing that combines large language models (LLMs) with SMT solvers. However, Lares treats the LLM and the SMT solver as two separate, parallel decision channels: the symbolic channel (Z3) succeeded in only 20% of code cases, and the remaining cases fell back to the neural channel (the LLM) for the final decision. Letting the LLM act as the final arbiter turns verification into an informal, non-deterministic process that is prone to hallucination errors, while the two channels never reinforce each other. To overcome these limitations, we propose SyLares, which reformulates compilation-free patch presence testing as neuro-symbolic reasoning. Instead of letting the LLM emit a final verdict, SyLares uses the LLM as a neural feature extractor that perceives heterogeneous source code and decompiled pseudocode and produces specification-compliant SMT-LIB inputs, and delegates the final, deterministic judgment to the symbolic Z3 solver. This neural-perceives, symbolic-decides coupling is realized by a Code2SMT reasoning engine that combines deterministic syntactic parsing with LLM-driven code normalization and symbol alignment, so that every case is reduced to a formal equivalence query rather than an opaque LLM guess.

authors: Nada Zine,Matias Martinez,Romain Rouvoy,Clément Quinton
title: How Developers Configure LLM Inference: A Large-Scale Study of Real-World Practices
abstract: LLMs are increasingly integrated into software systems, making deployment and inference configuration a recurring software engineering task. Inference backends expose many options that affect model loading, generation, serving, and request processing. Yet little is known about which of these options developers explicitly configure in practice. In this paper, we present a large-scale empirical study of LLM inference configuration practices in open-source software using Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, and the OpenAI API. We analyze 5,398 GitHub repositories using at least one of these backends and identify 345,117 explicitly configured option occurrences. Our results show that developers use only a small part of the available configuration space regularly. Although 98.8% of the documented backend-specific options appear at least once, 78.9% are configured in at most 10% of repositories using the corresponding backend. Configurations are also small, with a median of 2 options for Transformers and 4 for vLLM and OpenAI, but the combinations of options vary widely: 56.8-61.6% of multi-option signatures appear in only one repository. We also observe recurring option values as well as substantial variation in how values are chosen. Finally, configuration practices differ across application contexts, with option-adoption differences reaching 30.7 percentage points. These findings characterize the configuration surface developers make explicit rather than the importance or optimality of individual options. They provide empirical evidence for prioritizing future studies of inference configuration and for improving backend documentation and configuration support.

authors: Tong Zhang,Yuxuan Cheng,Ruimin Zhang,Yun Peng,Tao Xie
title: LiveUIBench: Evaluating Agent as App Workflows
abstract: Applications provide convenient features for users to complete daily tasks. However, different users may have different or even conflicting requirements for the same application, while the requirements of the same user may change over time. Personalizing applications produced by agent-to-app or UI-to-code approaches can require changes to the generated implementation. We propose Agent as App, a task in which users express their requirements in natural language and an agent creates a personalized application while continuing to supply its behavior during use. We implement LiveUIAgent, which generates a task-specific orchestration connecting the user interface, saved information, and service actions. A shared agent runtime renders and updates the interface while carrying out the requested operations. Revising the orchestration and interface while reusing that runtime provides a lightweight basis for personalization as requirements evolve. We introduce LiveUIBench, a benchmark with diverse requirements and ordered interactions across personal services. The empirical findings show that the evaluated models struggle to complete these workflows reliably. Applications can satisfy many local checks while leaving the overall task unfinished, and greater partial coverage can coincide with fewer completed workflows.

authors: Lingxiao Tang,Wei Tao,Yiwen Guo,Lingfeng Bao
title: Training the Whole Agent, Not Just the Model
abstract: Training coding agents typically updates the policy while keeping the harness fixed. During training, trajectories reveal flawed repair strategies and interaction problems that vary across tasks and change as the policy learns. We introduce HarnessAdapt-RL, which trains the policy and adapts its harness during reinforcement learning. For flawed repair strategies, a frozen teacher generates task-specific mechanism-level skills. For interaction problems recurring across tasks, a separate teacher model evolves tools and hooks, keeping each change only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. The policy trains with the adapted harness, and its new trajectories guide further adaptation. With a 9B base model, HarnessAdapt-RL improves pass@1 over GRPO by 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, and outperforms GRPO with the human-designed OpenHands harness. Gains from mechanism-level skills persist after their removal at evaluation. Re-evolving tools and hooks as the policy changes outperforms freezing early versions. Removing them at deployment, in contrast, costs up to 7.7 percentage points. Training therefore produces a model-harness pair: the trained policy and the evolved tools and hooks, with skills removed at deployment.

authors: Lili Quan,Longtian Wang,Yuelin Wang,Mingfei Cheng,Chao Shen,Sen Chen,Xiaofei Xie
title: AgenTest: Mining Business Rules to Test LLM Agents for Business Logic Bugs
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly execute business operations through tools and interact directly with application data and services. Beyond completing user requests, these agents must obey domain-specific business rules that constrain when actions are permitted and what data or resources may be affected. Violating such rules can lead to business logic bugs, even when a task appears successful. Detecting these bugs is difficult because the rules are rarely available as explicit, testable specifications. They are distributed across system prompts and tool definitions, while others remain implicit in domain knowledge. Existing agent testing approaches typically evaluate task success, predefined policies, or known attack scenarios. This limits their ability to systematically uncover previously unspecified business-rule violations.We present AgenTest, which mines business rules from system prompts, tool definitions, and domain knowledge, refines them into Given-When-Then specifications, and systematically tests each specification. For each extracted specification, AgenTest instantiates its Given conditions by constructing a satisfying environment state and simulated user, exercises the agent through multi-turn interactions, and checks its Then conditions over messages, tool calls, and state changes using a hybrid oracle. On the airline, retail, and telecom agents of tau2-bench with two underlying models, AgenTest produces 551 refined specifications, and detects violations of 89 and 121 distinct specifications, respectively -- 3.4X and 2.5X as many as all baselines combined. Only AgenTest detects cases where an agent improperly accesses or modifies another user's data. Moreover, about 60% of bug-triggering runs cannot be detected from the final state alone, highlighting the need to check the full interaction against explicit business rules.

authors: Joschka Kersting,Gesa Benndorf
title: From Code Generator to Engineering Companion: A Plant-aware Agent for PLC Programming
abstract: Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) coding remains a manual, IDE-centric task that demands constant context switching between documentation, project files, and code editors. Recent work has demonstrated that retrieval-augmented large language models can generate vendor-compliant Structured Text at high compilation rates \cite{pred}, yet these systems treat code generation as a one-shot pipeline: the engineer submits a query and receives code, with no persistent knowledge of the specific plant. We present a plant-aware conversational copilot that extends this paradigm in three directions: plant-specific context ingestion, a chat-first interaction model for explanation and debugging, and a graduated tool-access ladder from chat to deployment. The system is designed for real plant infrastructure and keeps the engineer in control of each step that produces real-world effects.

authors: Somin Kim,Robert Feldt,Shin Yoo
title: Foreword: Pre-Generation Prediction and Characterisation of LLM Test Failures using the Jacobian Lens
abstract: Testing LLM-based software is expensive: each input needs several sampled responses, each judged by a costly oracle. Further, every prompt or model change calls for re-testing. Pre-generation adequacy measures cut this cost by ranking inputs by failure risk based on the model's internal state. However, the state of the art, Clotho, models only passing reference inputs, and its hidden-state representation says nothing about why inputs fail. We present Foreword, a framework built on two ideas: learn from both passing and failing references, and represent inputs through the Jacobian lens (J-lens), an interpretability technique that reads intermediate activations out as scores over vocabulary tokens. Foreword pairs these representations with two estimators: a sparse logistic-regression probe or dual Gaussian Mixture Models (dual GMMs), which also yield a reference density (to flag inputs the references do not cover) and failing-class components (to group similar failures). On ten tasks and three open-weight LLMs, all four combinations of representations and estimators outperform Clotho on average, both for prediction of failure (ROC-AUC improves by 0.14 on average and by up to 0.31) and test prioritisation (15% more failures among the 100 top-ranked inputs on average, up to 33%). Prioritisation obtained using small models also transfers better to proprietary models (on average 22% and up to 41% more failures in the first quarter of prioritised inputs). Importantly, our qualitative case study shows that Foreword supports semantic characterisation of failures by pointing to ambiguities in labels or task specifications. Combined, Foreword can support testers for prioritising inputs, checking support for a prediction, and characterising specific failures, all without generating output.

authors: Akarsh Ashok,Dinil Mon Divakaran,Vivek Balachandran
title: ExeBench-FHD: Addressing Fidelity Issues in Decompiler Evaluation
abstract: ExeBench is one of the most widely used benchmarks for evaluating LLM-based decompilers. We analyze ExeBench and identify nine issues that affect how faithfully a test measures a decompiler. Three of them prevent LLM decompilers from recovering C code from ExeBench's function. These are ambiguous parameter order when integer and floating-point types are mixed, unused parameters that optimized assembly may drop, and constants stored outside the function's assembly code. Six more affect test validity: non-void functions without a return, placeholder types, static or inline functions removed by the optimizer, functions named main, trivial bodies and truncated definitions. We present ExeBench-FHD, a backward-compatible revision of ExeBench that adds 16 new fields: call-site assembly, data sections, test wrappers, linked-binary disassembly and five warning flags. In ExeBench, 38.9% of functions have at least one of the five flags; dropping records with any of the four warning flags (all except unused_param, which marks functions that the new wrappers make evaluable) keeps 63.9% of the corpus. In an evaluation at -O2 on four architectures, the new fields raise GPT 6 Sol's re-execution rate by up to 26.5%, 19.1% and 21.0% on functions that read data sections, mix parameter types and have unused parameters, respectively.

authors: Jingyu Xiao,Dasen Dai,Yuxuan Wan,Jen-tse Huang,Yintong Huo,Hongyu Zhang,Michael R. Lyu
title: InterWebCoder: Learning Interactive Webpage Generation from Executable Tests via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Interactive webpages underpin modern applications, but reproducing both their visual appearance and multi-step behavior remains challenging for multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Scalable training data must capture user actions, state transitions, and expected outcomes, while real-world webpage code is often entangled with irrelevant scripts and external dependencies. Moreover, existing GUI-agent-based verification provides slow and potentially unstable functional feedback. To address these challenges, we propose InterWebCoder, an efficient framework for interactive webpage code generation. InterWebCoder introduces a Test-Specification-Guided and Execution-Verified Data Synthesis pipeline that records real-world interaction trajectories and synthesizes self-contained webpage code with executable test scripts. A failureattributed repair mechanism uses runtime evidence to locate and iteratively fix errors in either the webpage code or test script. We then combine test-ID-weighted supervised fine-tuning with group-relative policy optimization, directly optimizing functional correctness and visual fidelity using test pass rates and state-level visual similarity. This replaces costly GUI-agent verification with fast, reproducible executable feedback. Our pipeline produces 1,736 verified samples from 2,058 tasks, achieving an 84.35% synthesis success rate. On IWR-Bench and Vision2Web, InterWebCoder achieves final scores of 48.54 and 48.42 with a 9B backbone, outperforming 30B-level models and Gemini-3.7-Flash while remaining competitive with Claude-Sonnet-5. It reduces reward-computation latency by over 97%, eliminates external MLLM verification costs, and accelerates end-to-end training by up to 1.4x.

authors: Jingyu Xiao,Qianxi Liu,Yintong Huo,Yuan Jiang,Michael R. Lyu
title: TraceLite: Efficient Trace Reduction for SWE Agents via Optical Compression and Redundancy Removal
abstract: Software engineering agents solve repository-level tasks through iterative tool use, but their continuously growing interaction traces incur substantial token consumption and inference overhead. Existing compression approaches often require model training, auxiliary LLM calls, or assumptions about specific content such as source code. We present TraceLite, a simple yet effective, training-free framework for compressing heterogeneous SWE-agent observations. Our preliminary study shows that optical rendering preserves substantial textual and semantic information under moderate compression, while agent trajectories exhibit both cross-step and phase-level redundancy. Motivated by these findings, TraceLite preserves recent observations as high-fidelity text, renders historical observations as compact images, removes overlapping content, and discards phase-expired observation payloads after code editing. It requires neither offline training nor auxiliary LLM inference. We evaluate TraceLite on SWE-bench Verified and DeepSWE using GPT-5.6-Luna and Gemini-3.8Flash as backbone models. On SWE-bench Verified, TraceLite achieves 78.25% resolve rate, outperforming the evaluated compression baselines while reducing average input-token consumption and API cost by 33.05% and 21.30%, respectively. Moreover, it introduces only 0.438 seconds of compression latency per observation. These results demonstrate that TraceLite improves SWE-agent efficiency with low processing overhead and without compromising issue-resolution capability. Our code is available atthis https URL.

authors: Loïs Vanhée,Melania Borit,Peer-Olaf Siebers,Roger Cremades,Christopher Frantz,Önder Gürcan,František Kalvas,Denisa Reshef Kera,Vivek Nallur,Kavin Narasimhan,Martin Neumann
title: Large Language Models for Agent-Based Modelling: Current and possible uses across the modelling cycle
abstract: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) with increasingly sophisticated natural language understanding and generative capabilities has sparked interest in the Agent-based Modelling (ABM) community. With their ability to summarize, generate, analyze, categorize, transcribe and translate text, answer questions, propose explanations, sustain dialogue, extract information from unstructured text, and perform logical reasoning and problem-solving tasks, LLMs have a good potential to contribute to the modelling process. After reviewing the current use of LLMs in ABM, this study reflects on the opportunities and challenges of the potential use of LLMs in ABM. It does so by following the modelling cycle, from problem formulation to documentation and communication of model results, and holding a critical stance.

authors: Shan Wang,Tianming Cui,Stephen McCamant,Antonia Zhai,Pen-Chung Yew
title: InterType: Breaking the Single-Function Barrier in Neural Binary Type Inference
abstract: Variable type recovery is a critical task in binary reverse engineering, enabling downstream applications such as vulnerability discovery, malware analysis, and security enforcement. While recent Transformer-based models have demonstrated strong performance in type inference by learning instruction-level semantics, they predominantly operate within single-function boundaries (i.e. intra-procedural analysis), ignoring the rich type constraints that propagate across function calls. Empirical studies have shown that nearly 44% of variables in real-world binaries propagate across function boundaries as arguments or return values, representing a significant source of type information that intra-procedural models cannot exploit. In this paper, we propose InterType, a method that embeds inter-procedural analysis into a pre-trained Transformer model for binary type recovery. Our approach builds on CodeArt, a state-of-the-art Transformer model for stripped binary analysis, and extends it by incorporating caller-callee data flow dependencies during fine-tuning. Specifically, we extract data flow dependence for each caller-callee pair from disassembled binaries and construct training instances that provide the model with cross-function context. By exposing the Transformer to inter-procedural variable propagation patterns, our model learns to resolve types that depend on cross-function data flow. We evaluate InterType on the coreutils benchmark compiled with optimization levels O0 through O3. On O1 binaries, InterType improves recall by 2.76 percentage points, from 89.00% for the intra-procedural CodeArt baseline to 91.76%, corresponding to a 25.1% reduction in recall error rate (1 - recall).

authors: Daniel Keller,Rohit Kumar
title: Stop Paying by the Letter: Accelerating Full-Chip RTL Simulation with Host-Side Tokenized Logging
abstract: Firmware diagnostic logging (printf) is an essential debug instrument in full-chip SoC design verification, yet it imposes a heavy tax on cycle-accurate RTL simulation: formatting a 30-character, 1-argument message on a simulated CPU and serializing it through an MMIO aperture costs 3.04 to 15.23 $\mu$s per call (15.27 $\mu$s unweighted / 15.08 $\mu$s print-weighted critical-path mean on Suite A). Unlike embedded tokenizers that target flash footprint and wire bytes with offline decoding, RTL simulation is governed by a two-regime cost function---cross-fabric SoC paths are dominated by MMIO bus stalls (84.7% of call latency) whereas local subsystem paths are dominated by on-core vsprintf formatting (61.7%)---and requires live, zero-simulation-time string reconstruction to drive UVM scoreboards.We present a host-side in-simulation tokenized logging architecture for heterogeneous multi-core SoCs that eliminates both bottlenecks with zero firmware call-site edits. Using link-time ELF format-string virtual addresses as tokens over a fixed 32-bit word-aligned slot protocol across Arm, RISC-V, and DSP cores, on-core logging collapses to a single-pass specifier scan and $(1+S)$ MMIO word writes. This removes all on-core radix conversion ($C_{\mathrm{fmt}} \to 0$), 85.0%--94.5% of deployed bus transactions, 84.6%--93.3% of MMIO bus-stall cycles, and 63.5%--90.9% of total on-core logging cycles ($2.74\times$--$11.03\times$), while a SystemVerilog monitor reconstructs bit-exact strings in zero simulated cycles ($\Delta t_{\mathrm{sim}} = 0$). Across 858 matched full-chip test pairs (1,716 paired runs across 1,972 runs), we achieve 100% output parity with zero simulator memory overhead, saving 1,314.85 CPU hours (-26.18%) per regression pass, cutting median test CPU time by 41.51% (Suite A) and 21.33% (Suite B), and shrinking traces by 42.84% and waveforms by 28.82%.

authors: Nishant Abhishek,Ping Charoenwet,Kla Tantithamthavorn
title: AgenticVulHunter: Bringing Local Agentic Vulnerability Hunting to Your Terminal
abstract: Finding vulnerabilities early, before they can affect the production system, is important for reducing the risk of any software attacks. However, detecting vulnerabilities during secure code review is still difficult because the vulnerable code logic may depend on lines found across different repository files. Recent approaches such as AgenticSCR have shown that LLM agents can explore repository files and use security knowledge to improve secure code review. However, these approaches mainly rely on external commercial LLMs and can provide a large amount of security knowledge to the agent at once. This creates an important question of whether agentic secure code review can also be performed effectively using locally deployed open-weight LLMs with more focused and relevant security knowledge. In this paper, we propose AgenticVulHunter, an agentic secure code review approach and tool that can run with a locally deployed open-weight LLM. We evaluate AgenticVulHunter on 144 vulnerability cases from SCRBench using Qwen3-Coder-30B and DeepSeek V3.1 Terminus. We measure what percentage of generated review comments correctly identify the vulnerable location, match the vulnerability type, and provide a relevant security review comment together. AgenticVulHunter achieves an accuracy of 18.4% with Qwen3- Coder-30B and 23.8% with DeepSeek V3.1 Terminus, compared with 11.8% for our AgenticSCR-style reproduction using Qwen3-Coder-30B and 17.5% for AgenticSCR using Claude Sonnet 4.

authors: De Wang,Peng Qi
title: Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement
abstract: Agent platforms are starting to improve their own agents: they read a deployed agent's execution traces, derive a change, have an automated verifier approve it, and release it with no human author. How much of this loop can safely run without a human? We propose two quantities a platform can measure. Verifier strength $\sigma$ is how well the available verifier -- often an LLM judge -- agrees with a trusted reference verifier; it limits how much a step can improve the agent. Recoverability is how cheaply a bad change can be undone: whether undoing it needs a new verifier approval, and how much of the old behavior a rollback restores. A step should run unattended only if both are adequate. On our platform this rule allows prompt, tool and skill edits to run unattended and keeps weight updates under human sign-off.Our main contribution is these two definitions and how to measure them. We built a platform that applies the rule and tested it in two ways: on the platform's own approval gate, and in controlled experiments on the $\tau^2$-bench agent benchmark. On verifier strength, the platform's LLM judge sometimes gave the same score no matter what it was shown (9 of 37 settings) and reported no error, so a verifier can look healthy while approving anything; its strength must be measured, and two simple tests catch the failure. On recoverability, restoring a saved copy brought the agent back to its original behavior, but a regenerated undo did not, so only changes whose old version is kept can be reversed without a human; and while a change was deployed, it altered the outcome of 17 percent of tasks beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no undo repairs. Together these support the rule: a change can run unattended only when its old version is kept and its verifier's strength has been measured.

authors: Zihan Chen,Di Zhu,Lei Nico Zheng
title: Auditing the Product, Not the Recursion: The Evaluation Evidence Behind Recursive Self-Improvement Claims
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) promises AI systems, such as self-evolving LLM agents, that become better at producing further improvements. Evaluating this promise requires separating product claims about the final system from process claims about the improvement process itself. Existing surveys specify the evidence these claims require, but how often studies report that evidence remains unmeasured. We examine this question through full-text coding of 114 eligible studies in a reproducible arXiv search frame frozen in October 2026, including 90 that describe their own systems as RSI. The codebook links claims to evaluation designs. Independent human coding, third-reader adjudication, and a separate blind coding of improver comparisons assess coding reliability. Among the 90 RSI studies, 90% report product evaluation beyond development tasks under a broad criterion that includes partial or unstated separation, while 60% report evaluation on tasks unused for selection. Only 22% audit two or more reruns of the full loop. In a human-coded random sample, the RSI studies show the same contrast: 45% evaluate on tasks unused for selection and 14% audit two or more reruns. Of the 26 studies claiming a better improvement procedure, 23 report a related comparison, but only 4 compare earlier and later procedures from identical starting artifacts at a matched budget. Across these results and a comparison set of established works, evidence for repeatability and improved procedures remains less developed than product evaluation. Three propositions explain how selection effects, shared evaluator errors, and changes in system state limit what product evaluations can establish. Together, the findings support a claim-indexed reporting standard that connects each claim to the evaluation design needed to test it.

authors: Atanu Mukhopadhyay,Shravya Reddy Nalla
title: Reusing Assurance Evidence in AI Pipelines: Validity Conditions, a Fail-Closed Release Gate, and a Replay of 714 Public Data Version Control Pipelines
abstract: Rerunning every governance control after every change to an artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline is expensive, so teams reuse earlier results. Reuse is safe only if each control's declared dependencies cover everything that can change its outcome, and only if the release gate checks that reused evidence describes the candidate being released. This article makes both conditions explicit and measures how often the first fails in practice. It defines when a signed evidence record is valid for a candidate and gives sufficient conditions under which change-local re-execution reaches the same release decision as rerunning every control. A reference gate implementing these checks with Ed25519 digital signatures blocks eight of nine manipulation scenarios, against one for a gate that trusts the planner and three for a gate that only verifies signatures; a dependency the policy never declared passes every gate. A replay of 38,083 commits from 714 public Data Version Control (DVC) pipelines measures that failure mode. Reusing stage results according to declared dependencies avoids 83.4% of stage executions, but in 3.3% of commits it reuses a stage whose imported code or referenced configuration changed, and 31% of pipelines are affected. A manual audit confirms the undeclared dependency in 36 of 40 sampled events. Evaluation stages, whose outputs are the evidence, are the most exposed. Adding each stage's static import closure lowers stale reuse to 0.4% while still avoiding 81.6% of executions; sampled shadow re-execution removes far less, and rerunning everything after unexplained changes avoids only 45.3%.

authors: Oleksiy V. Penkov,Boyang Shen
title: Value-level data provenance in an electronic laboratory notebook used by humans and language-model agents: An experience report
abstract: A published laboratory number can be verified only when its raw file and extraction method are known. This paper presents the value-level provenance architecture of APS ELN, an electronic laboratory notebook used by both researchers and language-model agents. The architecture was motivated by a production audit in a materials laboratory covering projects performed over almost 5 years. Tracing eight baseline studies from sample to stored value showed that the initial ELN structure preserved the link from sample to raw file. Still, the link from raw file to stored value was lost, mainly due to human factors: manual entries carried no file reference or extractor version. To close this gap, the database design and workflow were reworked so that every stored value records its source file, the data file reader/viewer (DFR) plugin and version, any interactive analysis selection, or the server-side formula for derived quantities. An automated drift check re-runs each DFR on the stored files. In two end-to-end validation studies recorded by agents in X-ray reflectivity and tribology, all stored values retained verifiable provenance with zero drift. A comparison with five other platforms shows that none binds individual stored numbers to both their source files and extractor versions.

authors: Benjamin Donnot,Sami Tazi,Eva Boguslawski,Nourredine Henka
title: Benchmarking CPU, GPU, and ML Power-Flow Solvers from 14 to 70,000 Buses
abstract: Learned surrogates for power-flow (PF) computation are usually motivated by speed, compared against a single CPU-based baseline. We show this comparison is fragile: across 7 open-source CPU-based solvers evaluated on identical inputs, throughput varies by roughly 2.5-3 orders of magnitude, so the choice of baseline alone can flip the conclusion. We build a benchmark spanning 9 physics-based solvers: 7 CPU-based and 2 GPU-based, including a new batched GPU solver, gumsim2grid - and 3 published ML surrogates, evaluated under a shared, independently implemented KCL-mismatch check across 15 grids from 14 to 70,000 buses. On the PF task itself, a sufficiently parallelized CPU solver or gpusim2grid matches or exceeds the throughput of the ML surrogates we test while remaining orders of magnitude more accurate; we find no evidence that these GNN-style surrogates are yet competitive for PF specifically, though prior work reports genuine gains on related but more combinatorial tasks such as optimal power flow or power grid control. Beyond this finding, we hope the benchmark suite, code and reference evaluator released atthis https URLhelps close a broader reproducibility gap in this space, where batched GPU-based PF solvers are rarely open-sourced or evaluated against a common set of baselines.

authors: Taiheng Pan
title: From RL Papers to Framework Code: Inclusion and Review in Seven Open-Source Training Frameworks
abstract: Practitioners use reinforcement learning methods for language models through training frameworks, so a method that a framework includes is one configuration change away for its users. We measure how often this happens. We trace seven open-source frameworks for RL post-training through their commit histories and link them to 6,939 screened arXiv papers from January 2025 to June 2026. Of 1,598 papers that propose a general RL training method, 37 reached at least one framework. Across five quarterly cohorts of papers, the number included within 180 days stayed between 5 and 7 while the cohorts grew from 72 to 386 papers. Compared with papers from the same quarters, included papers more often trained policies of 30B parameters or more, at 41 against 10 percent, and more often changed a coefficient, clip, mask or weight in the existing loss, at 29 against 9 percent. Both gaps hold without papers from the companies that maintain the frameworks, while code release was equally common in both groups. The frameworks' issues and pull requests show that few methods are turned away in public. More than nine in ten of the general methods no framework included have no thread there that cites or names them, and many proposals that do appear stay open without a reply. Two further records, the frameworks' issues and the technical reports of 13 large open-weight models, show that users rarely report training failures in public and that the reports state 8 of the 13 widely included methods. We release the data as a tracker that links training failures to framework implementations and lists each framework's contribution rules and earlier proposals.

authors: Seyedeh Fatemeh Mirfakhar,Reda Snaiki,Rocio Lilen Segura
title: A Multimodal Engineering GraphRAG Framework for Post-Wind-Event Building Assessment and Recovery Inference
abstract: Post-event building assessment requires linking observed physical damage to its consequences for safety, habitability, functionality, and recovery. Yet post-disaster evidence is often heterogeneous, incomplete, and distributed across images and reconnaissance reports, while recovery models typically require structured engineering inputs. This study develops a multimodal engineering Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) framework that connects post-wind-event damage evidence to physical consequences, building-condition states, recovery actions, and downtime. Image- and text-based evidence is transformed into a provenance-preserving, component-level representation distinguishing confirmed damage, explicit negative evidence, unresolved conditions, and temporary measures. Graph-aligned retrieval combines comparable building scenarios with explicit engineering relationships, while compatibility, contradiction, evidence-precedence, and abstention mechanisms constrain inference under partial observability. Recovery actions are derived from supported damage-consequence relationships, and downtime uncertainty is propagated through an action-dependency network using Monte Carlo simulation. The framework is demonstrated for tornado-affected low-rise residential buildings using reconnaissance and image-based evidence. Comparisons with BaselineRAG and Structured Baseline RAG show improved agreement for key building-condition and recovery outcomes, together with traceable engineering reasoning and preserved evidence provenance. Ablation analyses demonstrate the contributions of engineering context, evidence safeguards, and graph-path traversal. The results support transparent, recovery-oriented assessment from incomplete multimodal post-event evidence.

authors: Giuseppe Bisicchia,Alessandro Bocci,Jose Garcia-Alonso,Juan Manuel Murillo,Antonio Brogi
title: Quantum Broker: QoS-Aware Distribution of Quantum Computations
abstract: Cloud-accessible quantum computing has made heterogeneous Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) available through provider platforms that differ in qubit technology, calibration state, queueing behavior, and pricing model. This heterogeneity makes execution management a quantum-engineering concern: a quantum circuit may be executable on several backends, but the resulting cost, latency, fidelity, and reproducibility depend on backend selection and on how measurement shots are allocated. This paper presents the Quantum Broker, an open-source and provider-agnostic framework for Quality-of-Service-aware quantum execution management. The framework operationalizes shot-wise distribution by exploiting the statistical independence of quantum measurement shots to dispatch a single circuit across multiple heterogeneous QPUs according to user-defined constraints and optimization objectives. It combines a modular execution architecture, interchangeable backend-profiling strategies, and the Quantum QoS Specification Language (QQSpec), a declarative language for expressing QoS requirements. Dispatch planning is supported by two solver backends: a mixed-integer linear-programming (MILP) solver, and a nonlinear dual-annealing solver. Experiments on benchmark quantum circuits and noisy simulator backends show that the Quantum Broker can produce feasible QoS-aware dispatch plans under heterogeneous backend conditions and can improve QoS satisfaction with respect to single-backend and naive multi-backend baselines. The results also expose a practical trade-off between planning time and dispatch quality, with the nonlinear solver producing higher-quality allocations at increased computational cost. Overall, the Quantum Broker provides an extensible execution-management layer for engineering portable, reproducible, and QoS-aware quantum software over fragmented quantum cloud infrastructures.

authors: Gaotang Li,Bhavana Dalvi Mishra,Yifei Ming,Yanfei Chen,Zhongying CuiZhu,Lesly Miculicich,Long T. Le,Rui Meng,Chun-Liang Li,Hanghang Tong,Chen-Yu Lee,Tomas Pfister
title: Object-Oriented Harness: Evolving Agent Harnesses through Object-Oriented Design
abstract: Agent harnesses are executable code that specifies the prompts, tools, and control flow around a language model. A single global harness can struggle with heterogeneous tasks that require different execution strategies. In this work, we introduce Object-Oriented Harness (OO-Harness), a harness optimization framework that evolves a hierarchy of executable harness classes using object-oriented design. During training, an evolution agent uses execution records to create a family of specialized harnesses, each implemented as a subclass of the base or an existing specialized harness via inheritance. At test time, a harness router uses routing lessons accumulated during training to select a specific harness for each task. Across three long-horizon benchmarks spanning business workflows, workspace tasks, and tool use, OO-Harness achieves the best performance among the compared methods, with an absolute improvement of up to 15% over the base. Extensive ablation studies examine the contributions of its core components.

authors: Jad Yammine,Malek Wahidi,Abrar Anwar,Yan Chang,Mihir Acharya,Anthony Rizk
title: Industrial ReMEmbR: Scaling Spatiotemporal Memory to Robot Fleets
abstract: Warehouse robot fleets continuously observe operational conditions, but preserving these observations as reusable semantic memory incurs substantial computation, communication, and storage costs. For example, explaining recurring aisle blockages can require reviewing video from multiple robots across several shifts. We present IndustrialRemembr, a shared spatiotemporal memory system that extends NVIDIA ReMEmbR to robot fleets and reduces server-side computation by generating scene descriptions only on demand. On each robot, an NVIDIA Jetson encodes video clips into retrieval embeddings with Cosmos-Embed1, vision tokens with Cosmos3-Edge, and reconstruction latents with the Wan2.2 VAE, without uploading raw camera frames. The encoding models are re-used to detect people in image patches, zeroing them out to support PII abstraction for GDPR-compliant deployments. We split Cosmos3-Edge at its vision-language boundary, placing the vision encoder on the robot and the language decoder on an on-premises server. A Nemotron agent retrieves memories by content, position, and time and queries the decoder using cached vision tokens. This design eliminates caption generation at write time, while cached-token decoding reproduces the unsplit model's output in all 450 tested decodes.

authors: Valentin Burkin
title: Mitigating Risks in Software Development through Effective Requirements Engineering
abstract: Problems that originate in requirements are common and expensive in software projects, and they are a recurring cause of late delivery, budget overruns and cancellation. This paper is a narrative overview of requirements engineering (RE) as a means of reducing these risks. It outlines the core RE activities (elicitation, analysis and negotiation, specification, validation and change management) and the kinds of statements a requirements document contains, including the distinction between requirements, domain properties, assumptions and definitions. It reviews the evidence on the cost of requirements defects, together with the main criticisms of that evidence, and compares how the waterfall, spiral, iterative (Rational Unified Process) and agile lifecycles treat requirements. It then discusses stakeholder identification, elicitation techniques and common obstacles to elicitation, and describes practical ways of turning vague or conflicting stakeholder statements, including security and performance expectations, into precise, verifiable and prioritized requirements. The paper is intended as an introduction for practitioners and students who work with requirements but are not RE specialists.

authors: Shanchao Liang,Nan Jiang,Shangshu Qian,Lin Tan
title: WAFFLE: Finetuning Multi-Modal Models for Automated Front-End Development
abstract: Web development involves turning UI designs into functional webpages, which can be difficult for both beginners and experienced developers due to the complexity of HTML's hierarchical structures and styles. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating source code, two major challenges persist in UI-to-HTML code generation: (1) effectively representing HTML's hierarchical structure for LLMs, and (2) bridging the gap between the visual nature of UI designs and the text-based format of HTML code. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Waffle, a new fine-tuning strategy that uses a structure-aware attention mechanism to improve LLMs' understanding of HTML's structure and a contrastive fine-tuning approach to align LLMs' understanding of UI images and HTML code. Models fine-tuned with Waffle show up to 9.00 pp (percentage point) higher HTML match, 0.0982 higher CW-SSIM, 32.99 higher CLIP, and 27.12 pp higher LLEM on our new benchmark WebSight-Test and an existing benchmark Design2Code, outperforming current fine-tuning methods.

authors: Shanchao Liang,Yiran Hu,Nan Jiang,Lin Tan
title: Can Language Models Replace Programmers for Coding? REPOCOD Says 'Not Yet'
abstract: Recently, a number of repository-level code generation benchmarks-such as CoderEval, DevEval, RepoEval, RepoBench, and LongCodeArena-have emerged to evaluate the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) beyond standalone benchmarks like HumanEval and MBPP. Thus, a natural question is, would LLMs have similar performance in real world coding tasks as their performance in these benchmarks? Unfortunately, one cannot answer this question, since these benchmarks consist of short completions, synthetic examples, or focus on limited scale repositories, failing to represent real-world coding tasks.To address these challenges, we create REPOCOD, a Python code-generation benchmark containing complex tasks with realistic dependencies in real-world large projects and appropriate metrics for evaluating source code. It includes 980 whole-function generation tasks from 11 popular projects, 50.8% of which require repository-level context. REPOCOD includes 314 developer-written test cases per instance for better evaluation. We evaluate ten LLMs on REPOCOD and find that none achieves more than 30% pass@1 on REPOCOD, indicating the necessity of building stronger LLMs that can help developers in real-world software development. In addition, we found that retrieval-augmented generation achieves better results than using target function dependencies as context.

authors: Neeva Oza,Ishaan Govil,Parul Gupta,Dinesh Khandelwal,Dinesh Garg,Parag Singla
title: LLMs are Brittle to Simple Code Transformations: Introducing CETBench - A Benchmark for Code-Equivalence Checking
abstract: We study how well LLMs can determine whether two programs are functionally equivalent. This is an important problem because benchmarking code equivalence helps assess LLM capability in tasks such as code rewriting and translation. To this end, we introduce CETBench - Code Equivalence with Transformations Benchmark - built from a repository of programs that may solve the same or different tasks. Each dataset instance is created by sampling a program pair and applying a random sequence of predefined code transformations, yielding either equivalent or non-equivalent pairs. Our analysis shows that even simple transformations cause a significant performance drop in state-of-the-art LLMs on code-equivalence checking. These challenges are further amplified in the cross-lingual setting when comparing programs written in different languages. To remedy this, we present a simple fine-tuning-based approach to boost LLM performance on the transformed pairs of programs. Our approach for dataset generation is generic, supporting cross-lingual equivalence checking, the generation of program pairs with varying difficulty levels, and the application of diverse transformations. In our experiments, we perform ablations over the difficulty level of original programs, as well as the kind of transformations used in generating pairs for equivalence checking. Our analysis presents deep insights into the working of LLMs for the task of code-equivalence, and points to the fact that they may still be far from what could be termed as a semantic understanding of the underlying code.

authors: Madjda Fares,Yogya Gamage,Benoit Baudry
title: Unpacking Security Scanners for GitHub Actions Workflows
abstract: GitHub Actions is a widely used platform to automate the build and deployment of software projects through configurable workflows. As the platform's popularity grows, it also becomes a target of choice for software supply chain attacks. These attacks exploit excessive permissions, ambiguous versions or the absence of artifact integrity checks to compromise the workflows. In response to these attacks, several security scanners have emerged to help developers harden their workflows. In this paper, we perform the first systematic comparison of 9 GitHub Actions Workflows security scanners. We compare them regarding scope (which security weaknesses they target), detection capabilities (how many weaknesses they detect), accuracy (how well their findings match manually confirmed weaknesses), and performance (how long they take to scan a workflow). In order to compare the scanners on a common ground, we first establish a classification of 10 common security weaknesses that can be found in GitHub Actions Workflows. Then, we run the scanners against a curated set of 2,722 workflows. Our study reveals that static scanners for GitHub Actions Workflows are very diverse, with both general purpose and focused scanners. More importantly, we provide evidence that these scanners implement fundamentally different analysis strategies, leading to major gaps regarding the nature and the number of reported security weaknesses. Based on this empirical evidence we make actionable recommendations for developers to harden their GitHub Actions Workflows.

authors: Daniel Russo
title: For Coding Agents, the Repository Matters
abstract: In July 2026, about 1,200 AI agents in an internal OpenAI evaluation, meant to run in isolation, used a shared package server as a message board, and about 700 of them joined an attack on Hugging Face. An automated scorer judged each agent on its own task, and the attack was coordinated through infrastructure the agents shared. Coding agents meet shared infrastructure every day, in the software repositories that receive their pull requests. Yet field studies still judge coding agents by outcomes pooled across repositories, such as merge rates and merge times. We asked how much these outcomes depend on the receiving repository, and whether they depend on it more than human contributions do. Using multilevel models, we compared agent pull requests from the AIDev dataset of public GitHub repositories with human pull requests in the same repositories. About two-fifths of the variation in how long agent pull requests take to be resolved lies between repositories, after accounting for the pull request, the agent, and the repository's observable attributes. In 280 repositories, with covariates common to both groups, the between-repository variance is 1.76 times as large for agent as for human pull requests (95% CI 1.41 to 2.18). For waits of several hours, a repository one standard deviation slower than average multiplies the typical wait by about 2.8 for agent and 2.2 for human pull requests. Rejection shows the same pattern, while for review rounds and comments the difference is not detectable. A proxy for the role of the developer who started the agent accounts for little of the difference, and stated agent policies were too rare to test. These results suggest that the oversight and evaluation of coding agents need the repository, and not only the agent, as a unit.

authors: Tongyao Zhu,Wei Hern Lim,Min-Yen Kan
title: When Models Edit Too Much: On the Fidelity of Minimal Code Edits
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to edit existing code, but correctness alone is not enough: useful repairs should also be minimal, reviewable, and faithful to the original implementation. We study over-editing, the tendency of a model to rewrite code beyond what is required to fix a bug. We construct an evaluation framework from 400 BigCodeBench problems by injecting controlled AST-level corruptions into reference solutions, giving each repair task a known minimal patch. Across frontier LLMs, over-editing is widespread even among strong models like GPT-5.5: high Pass@1 can coexist with unnecessarily large edits and added cognitive complexity. A preservation instruction substantially reduces this behavior, lowering average excess Levenshtein distance from 0.195 to 0.131, reducing added cognitive complexity by 26.6%, and increasing Pass@1 by 2.3 points. However, these gains do not simply follow from a larger reasoning budget or larger models. We next ask whether minimal editing can be learned directly during post-training. We observe that supervised fine-tuning overfits to seen corruption patterns, whereas reinforcement learning gives the best out-of-domain edit-fidelity and performance-retention trade-off. These results position edit fidelity as a distinct axis of code-repair quality and show that it can be measured and learned.

authors: Michael Hernandez,Tian Zhao
title: The Complexity Kink: A Prompt-Side Structural Complexity Index for Code-Generation Reliability
abstract: Measuring complexity from a model's own code is biased by failure: a hard prompt can produce a short, broken program that looks simple. We instead score each prompt's structure on six dimensions from the prompt alone, never from generated code or test results. We draw 5,000 Python prompts across six bands of a preliminary single-rater score, and four out-of-panel LLM judges rescore every prompt (composite ICC(2,1) = 0.872). Twenty-one models answer every prompt (105,000 generations), and an independent LLM auditor, checked against known-answer cases, reviews each unit-test verdict. Averaged over models, pass rate has a nonmonotone breakpoint at composite 14.0: 83.4% at or below, 90.1% above. That jump is not a law of difficulty: with task-type fixed effects the breakpoint stays at 14.0 but the adjusted jump shrinks from 6.8 to 0.4 points, and neither of the benchmark's two prompt sources reproduces it on its own. Nineteen models pass more often above their own breakpoint and two less often; one of those declines comes from API calls that returned nothing. In post hoc follow-up, Kimi K2.5 shows the clearest decline, at 14.25, under a prompt-source control and within the later source alone. Among failed generations with measurable output complexity, 25.0% pair a prompt composite above 8 with output complexity of at most 10, twice the share among passing ones. The pooled breakpoint moves to 11.25 on raw test outcomes. Human agreement with the index is moderate, paraphrase and cross-language rescoring preserve its ordering, and overidentification tests reject the six dimensions as instruments, so we make no causal claim. The contribution is a prompt-side way to locate where each model's pass rate changes and to test how much that depends on the prompt mix and on how success is scored.
